artifacts.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

artifacts.synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

artifacts.synopsis: Northern California Presbytery adopted an abstract resolution declaring six different views on the diaconate permissible for ministers and Sessions; the SJC sustained the complaints and annulled the resolution, holding that no court may issue binding abstract decrees beyond its proper jurisdictional exercise. A concurring opinion analyzed each of the six diaconal views in detail and set out standards (the GUMP/Kniseley framework) for when diaconal assistant practices are constitutionally permissible.

artifacts.synopsis: On complaint from TE David Kniseley and others, the SJC reviewed Rocky Mountain Presbytery's refusal to forbid a mission church from giving an unordained female staff member the title 'Minister of Church Life.' The SJC denied the complaint. It held the BCO uses 'minister' synonymously with pastor and teaching elder, but is silent on general use for non-ordained staff; a lower court may exercise discretion subject to BCO 40-2(3)'s WESP review. The decision addressed only the constitutional issue, not the title's wisdom or propriety; four commissioners dissented.
